items.question: How did your work on police use of facial recognition shape your view of the importance of understanding machine learning?
items.object: Police use of facial recognition and public understanding of machine learning
items.answer: I spent a year at Georgetown Law. This was kind of a year in between my master’s and my PhD, and I spent a year there working on technology policy. I think what I already saw at that time was that AI, or at least machine learning, was starting to become a force to be reckoned with in the policy world. I worked on police use of facial recognition, which today sounds pretty basic in some sense compared to what we do, but then was kind of still novel and still something that people didn’t fully understand. I remember the Seattle Police Department had FAQs on its website about their facial recognition system. One of which was, “Isn’t this biased?” And the answer was, “It’s an algorithm. It can’t see race,” which sounds very silly today, but then, based on what people knew, especially in the popular consciousness, was not a ridiculous thing to say. So it kind of became clear to me that I had to know more about this topic, and that was part of my motivation actually to go back to grad school.

items.question: How did your approach to testing ideas in deep learning shape the development of the lottery ticket hypothesis?
items.object: The experimental approach behind the lottery ticket hypothesis
items.answer: It was actually really simple at the end of the day. I was reading some papers on pruning. The topic kind of caught my eye as something that was interesting: can we understand these things better? Can we get down to their essence, what these neural networks are doing? Things that never really came to be in pruning, but at the time again sounded very reasonable. From there, I just asked this really dumb question: why can we only prune networks at the end of training? And asked a faculty member at MIT, who gave me a dumb answer. It made me want to go and study, made me want to go and ask some basic questions that could be scientifically answered with experiments. I was pretty frustrated with the fact that we say so much in the deep learning literature, and it’s still true today, that’s just unsubstantiated. There’s no evidence behind it; it’s just an intuition or received wisdom or something like that. I wanted to go and pose a bunch of hypotheses and test them. One of them was what kind of became the lottery ticket hypothesis. It was called that at the time; there were just a bunch of different hypotheses, and that was one of them. I tested it, and on very tiny networks, like one-hidden-layer networks for XOR, it seemed to work. From there, the rest is history to some extent.

items.question: How do you decide what counts as knowledge in deep learning research?
items.object: Evidence and knowledge in deep learning research
items.answer: It’s pretty simple for me: data. I believe nothing until I see the data in front of me. In fact, I often believe nothing until I’ve reproduced that data myself, because I’ve seen a lot of circumstances in which seemingly very clever papers have cooked the books, intentionally or unintentionally. I don’t mean to accuse people, but have failed to run an ablation or have picked a really easy baseline—things that I think we do unconsciously because we really want our experiments to work. So we will often find ways to make it seem like they work to us, and then we get ourselves into trouble sometimes. There are a bunch of papers—I don’t like to name names on this stuff, just because it’s a lot of students, and I’ve been a student. I understand that at the end of the day, you should be allowed to make mistakes and not get publicly punished for it—but there are a lot of papers that I’ve seen that I have not been able to reproduce for the life of me. It’s very frustrating. It’s a sad state for the literature to be in. It’s really knowledge: what you can show with evidence. And what you can show when you—you know, we can go back to Karl Popper and falsifiability, if you want—it is when you try very hard to falsify an idea and can’t. That is knowledge.

items.question: How do you think about Karl Popper’s approach to scientific inquiry in your own work?
items.object: Karl Popper’s approach to scientific inquiry
items.answer: I’m a big Popper fan when it comes to this. At some point during my PhD, I sat down and read Popper because I felt like I needed to understand what science was better if I was going to make claims about it. For me, it really is all about, you know, hypothesis, attempt to falsify, hypothesis, attempt to falsify, and the only thing that matters is: did it work?

items.question: How do you judge the value of theory and mathematical proofs as ways to establish knowledge?

items.answer: I don’t care about the theory. I don’t care about your fancy math. I just want to know: did it work? It’s useless, quite frankly.

items.question: How do you evaluate your original lottery ticket hypothesis paper as an example of the scientific approach you value?
items.object: The lottery ticket hypothesis as a scientific contribution
items.answer:
I wouldn’t look at the lottery ticket hypothesis as the end-all-be-all of great work on this front. The reason I say that is because it was the first attempt at this, and a lot of this philosophy is post hoc in some sense, looking back and trying to do better work in the future. I will not claim that the lottery ticket hypothesis is my best work. Far from it, it’s my worst work. It was my earliest work. I think it’s pretty important to emphasize that from the beginning. I know it’s looked at as a popular paper these days. That doesn’t mean it’s my best work, far from it, and I think the work that I did a lot later in my PhD reflected the best of these ideas.

Pretty simply, it’s a hypothesis about the fact that there exist these smaller networks that can be trained. The biggest challenge there is it’s not really a falsifiable hypothesis. That’s kind of the big flaw, because in order to falsify it, we’d have to look at every single subnetwork and show that none of them have this property. Practically speaking, it’s non-falsifiable. That’s something that I’m critical of myself for. From there, I go through and try to find existential evidence to support this hypothesis. It’s really an existential statement, not a universal statement. The way that you justify it is with more existential evidence. It’s non-falsifiable: I can’t show that a network lacks these things practically, and I can’t show that all networks contain them. In some sense, it doesn’t really follow the best practices that Popper would describe. I wish I were making a more universal statement as opposed to an existential statement, but science isn’t perfect and you make the best with what you’ve got.

items.question: Why do you favor two-sided research questions in your neural network research?
items.object: Two-sided research questions
items.answer:
This is advice I give to PhD students all the time: ask two-sided questions. That is to say, ask questions where no matter what result you get, you learn something about the world. I have a follow-up paper to the lottery ticket hypothesis where I look at neural network training and the optima that they end up in, and ask the question: at what point in training is the optimum determined? It’s a cool question because one hypothesis is maybe it’s determined from initialization. Cool, that would be interesting. Maybe it’s undetermined until the very last step of training, but that last step of training probably isn’t going to bring you to a different optimum. So the answer has to be somewhere in the middle. I love that because it’s a measurement question. There’s a phenomenon I want to measure, and no matter what I find, I’m going to gain knowledge and learn something. Those are my favorite kinds of questions to ask these days.

It is a guaranteed paper if you ask a good question no matter what the result is. So if you’re a PhD student out there, I love my two-sided questions. I encourage students to work on it because it takes all the stress of “will this work or not?” away. It limits what you can ask to a certain extent, but honestly, I think you can refactor most questions into a two-sided question. The original lottery ticket paper was not a two-sided question. I got lucky that it worked, because it could have been that I just couldn’t find these things, or maybe they did exist, maybe they didn’t; maybe I had a method to find them, maybe I didn’t, and I could have just gone home with nothing. That follow-up question—when does the network end up, and when is the optimum determined?—is a great two-sided question. I really try hard to ask those in my papers these days.

items.question: How would you approach exploratory research questions like the original lottery ticket hypothesis today?
items.object: Exploratory research questions such as the original lottery ticket hypothesis
items.answer: In some sense, you can either look at this and go, “Wow, today I wouldn’t even ask that question,” and today I might ask that question, but my belief is that if I were to ask that question, I’d want to ask it very cheaply and very quickly. There are lots of questions like this, lots of hypotheses, lots of conjectures of “Wouldn’t it be cool if blank worked?” Those are great questions to ask, but I see PhD students getting caught up in asking a million of those and then taking two months to try to answer each one, and then you end up with nothing. The answer at that point is, if you’re going to ask those kinds of questions, it’s about efficiency. It is about how quickly you can possibly get through all these experiments.

items.question: How do you view the unapologetically empirical approach you took in the lottery ticket paper?
items.object: The empirical scientific approach of the lottery ticket paper
items.answer: I was unashamed of that approach largely because I didn’t realize there were that many other approaches or people had different opinions, because I was new to this. It is just completely unapologetic empiricism, and only empiricism. There is not a theorem in that paper; there’s not an attempt at a theorem in that paper. In the original version that got accepted, there was no mathematical notation to describe the hypothesis, and eventually my adviser made me add it. It is unapologetic about how it looks at the world in that approach. I continue to be deeply unapologetic about empiricism.

items.question: How do you think credit should be assigned among the authors of a research paper?
items.object: Credit allocation among authors of research papers
items.answer: I think there’s a bad habit we have of looking at the author who we know best, not the author who actually did the work. Author ordering: just because Yoshua Bengio is on a paper does not mean Yoshua Bengio did a damn thing for that paper. In the same way that just because I’m on a paper doesn’t mean I did anything for it. Look for the first author and maybe look for the last author, but credit where credit is due to the students who worked on it. With this paper, I’m not the first author; Alex Renda is, and this is his work. I want to emphasize that from the start. This is not my work. I’m supporting cast, but this is Alex Renda and all the hard work he did.

items.question: What do you think Alex Renda’s paper comparing rewinding and fine-tuning reveals about the relevance of lottery tickets to neural network pruning in general?
items.object: Alex Renda’s paper comparing rewinding and fine-tuning in neural network pruning
items.answer: Alex’s work is really about this question: lottery tickets are all about finding networks early in training, or at the beginning of training, that can train to completion sparse. A good follow-up question to ask is: are these just better-pruned networks in general? We were really focused on, can we train sparse networks? There was no competition for this algorithm right now, or at least there is now, but at the time there wasn’t, for finding these sparse networks that could train. But are sparse networks that you find at the beginning of training competitive with networks you find at the end of training, the traditional way that you prune? This paper says, well, sort of. It’s not clear-cut, but they’re not far off. There is this important question: when you go back to the beginning of training, you’re doing two things. One is that you’re taking the weights back to an early state, maybe you’re kind of keeping the network centered. The other is that you’re redoing the whole learning rate schedule. You are training the network starting at a high learning rate again and then going back down to a low learning rate. We asked: can you decouple these? Is the learning rate more important than the rewinding of the weights, or what? The answer was really the learning rates mattered. When we prune a network, even at the end of training, we should go back to this higher learning rate, give the network some time to recover. There are all sorts of hypotheses as to why this might happen, and, again, no hypothesis matters until you’ve gone and actually tested it. It was a neat observation that maybe we were able to learn something from the lottery ticket results that were relevant to pruning in general, not just to lottery tickets.

items.question: What do you think remains unresolved about why learning rate rewinding works better after pruning?
items.object: Why learning rate rewinding works better after pruning
items.answer: We didn’t get time to study it, really. We didn’t get time to look at the loss landscape after you do learning rate rewinding and not weight rewinding. It was something that we just didn’t have time to get into, and we all had other projects to move on to. It’s a question that I think has been studied a little bit in the community, but honestly I haven’t seen a definitive answer. I’d still love it if somebody went and studied what happens on the loss landscape when you play with this learning rate schedule after pruning. Do the networks really end up in different places? Why does learning rate rewinding work better? Can we try to make any statement about this? All that the paper showed was that it does work better. That’s it. As to why, we’ll have to figure that out.

items.question: Why do you favor anchoring your pruning strategy in prior work when studying neural-network pruning?
items.object: Conservative pruning strategies and experimental design choices anchored in prior work
items.answer: I took a really very conservative strategy in the lottery ticket paper because I didn’t want it to be about the pruning algorithm; I wanted it to be about the results. Don’t try to maximize efficiency, just try to get a result. In this paper, we really wanted to just, again, get a clean result. In the publication process, if you change anything about a strategy that differs from prior work, someone will ask you a hard question about why you did that, because it’s right to accuse you of cooking the books. Did you make that choice differently because quietly that choice was necessary for your stuff to work? If you hadn’t made that choice, would things have still worked? It is always a good practice—and for any PhD student out there—to anchor any choices you make in something that happened in prior work. If you do that, then you basically have a get-out-of-jail-free card for the design choices you make. We did that in this paper. We didn’t want to play around with changing the pruning algorithm or with other pruning algorithms, at least initially, because we wanted to make sure that what we did was defensible.

items.question: How did you approach testing the idea that early-training SGD noise explains why the lottery ticket algorithm sometimes fails at initialization?
items.object: Measuring early-training SGD noise in the paper on linear mode connectivity and the lottery ticket hypothesis
items.answer: Carolina was central in everything that happened in this paper, and a lot of the key ideas are hers. It’s important to again clarify that. The paper came about from a conversation between Carolina and me where I had observed recently that, in cases where the lottery ticket algorithm wasn’t working at initialization, it was working very early in training. We talked again about hypotheses for why this might be happening. Maybe there’s something very noisy about SGD early in training that scrambles the weight so much that initialization doesn’t matter anymore. The question is: how do you substantiate that? That’s a very fuzzy hypothesis. One way of dealing with all this SGD noise would be lower the learning rate a bunch, and so we tried that, and that actually worked. That gave you lottery tickets again—worse lottery tickets, but lottery tickets nonetheless. Then you try learning rate warm-up: what if you have the learning rate low early in training and high later in training? That worked too, suggesting that maybe there really is something early in training. But you still need to measure this effect. You need some way to say, how do you measure SGD noise? A lot of people love to look at things like the variance of the gradients or the magnitude of the gradients, but that’s kind of descriptive; it doesn’t really tell you anything concrete about the final network. We came around eventually—and this is Carolina’s idea—to: let’s look at the outcome of optimization. Does changing the noise early in training affect the outcome of optimization in a meaningful way? In this case, the outcome was: what optimum does it end up in?

items.question: Why do you prefer examining one-dimensional slices when trying to understand a neural network’s loss landscape?
items.object: One-dimensional slices of neural-network loss landscapes
items.answer: Take a network and try training it multiple times. Fix a network—it could be at the beginning of training or sometime during training—make a bunch of copies of it and train those copies on different random seeds. That is, change the data order, sample your data differently, sample new data augmentation. Where do they land? Do they land in the same convex region or different convex regions? The way that you figure that out is you just take two copies and start looking at the loss landscape between them. If it’s flat, cool, they’re in the same convex region. If there’s a spike, there’s a barrier between them. It’s these, in some sense, one-dimensional slices of the loss landscape that end up being very helpful for trying to make sense of it. The loss landscape is this ultra-high-dimensional thing, and I don’t think any attempt to visualize it is very productive. You’re taking this high-dimensional thing and trying to compress it down to something much smaller. I don’t know if that really works; you’re losing a lot of information. What I like here is you’re taking these one-dimensional slices. These are high-fidelity; you’re looking at the loss landscape, just looking at these very tiny, narrow slices of a very high-dimensional space. They happen to be important slices because they relate two different networks to each other.

items.question: What makes checking whether trained networks occupy the same convex region of the loss landscape a meaningful metric to you?
items.object: Sharing a convex region of the loss landscape as a metric for comparing trained networks
items.answer: The answer is honestly, well, it seems to have some descriptive power and it seems to distinguish networks that have different properties in other ways. It seemed to work here, and it seems to work in a bunch of other places. It’s become a popular way of distinguishing things. You could end up in a way that, for example, maybe everything is in the same convex region at the end of training, which is true for small, fully connected networks on MNIST. You do kind of see this: everything ends up in basically the same convex region, so it doesn’t matter too much. But in larger networks, thankfully, it doesn’t, and so this is a meaningful metric. The other cool thing about it is it tells you when you can average networks and get a useful artifact out the other end. That’s been something that people have built on.

items.question: How do you judge whether a metric is a useful way to measure something in machine learning?
items.object: Evaluating measurement metrics in machine learning
items.answer: I think there’s not really a clear way to do this. This is why the way that you measure things is a little artisanal. I wish there were a clear razor there, and it’s something that I haven’t ever figured out, a clean way to handle. If you want to really dig into my papers and rip them apart, look at the way I measure things and tell me that’s a dumb way of measuring things. But I think this is a problem that affects the whole field to some extent. When we deal with generative models, we still don’t know how to measure what a good generative model is. We still have no idea. I think this is in some sense an unsolved problem. At the end of the day I look for things that are non-vacuous. Measuring whether networks are in the same linearly connected region would have been vacuous if every network were in the same linearly connected region or no networks are in the same linearly connected region. I look for things that are non-vacuous.

items.question: What did your work on scaling laws for neural network pruning teach you about getting scaling laws right?
items.object: Getting scaling laws for neural network pruning right
items.answer: My takeaway here was that, in addition to the fact that a lot of things are predictable—and I hope the paper conveys this—getting scaling laws right is hard. It is very easy on a log-log plot to get things that look like they kind of fit, but actually doing the hard work of evaluating whether things work and figuring out why a scaling law is right or wrong—I hope the paper brings that out a little bit. I hope the paper emphasizes just how much trickiness and finesse there is in getting it to work, because it’s not easy. I really hope we told that story too, because it’s so easy for people to fit something to a log-log plot and say, “Ah yes, I have described it,” but the little details matter so much.

items.question: How do you judge whether methods claiming to find lottery tickets early in neural network training have actually succeeded?
items.object: Evaluating methods that claim to find lottery tickets early in neural network training
items.answer: The question is how you measure. I think this paper established what I consider to be the right way of evaluating whether something has really found neural networks at initialization, or at any point in training, that are as good as what you can find post hoc using highly inefficient lottery ticket methods. The short answer is none of these papers held up under scrutiny. Partially, they were no better than some really dumb, naive methods that they didn’t test against, and partially because when you started to try to falsify the logic behind which these methods came about, some of them just completely collapsed. One of the methods in the paper, I tried pruning the opposite of what the paper said to prune and got the same results, which should tell you that any justification the authors claimed for this method—you could justify anything with that. Again, it’s a falsifiability question.

items.question: How do you view the role of papers that scrutinize and challenge other researchers’ claims in lottery ticket research?
items.object: Critical papers and scientific accountability in lottery ticket research
items.answer: At the end of the day, this is me trying to hold up some papers that made very expansive claims to scrutiny and finding that I think they all withered away under the kind of scientific scrutiny that we should all apply to our own papers. I want to be careful in the words I choose because these were papers written by students, and I want to respect that. But I do think there was not enough of an attempt to falsify their own results. On the one hand, I don’t think these were the world’s best contributions to the scientific literature. On the other hand, that means you open yourself up to someone writing a paper like this that’s in some sense a takedown paper. I tried not to write it as a takedown paper because I think those are mean-spirited, but it is in some sense an attempt to bring some scientific order and attempts at falsification to a space where people were exercising some wishful thinking in their papers. In some sense, now that I’m kind of the police officer walking the beat on the lottery ticket space, it’s my job to occasionally write one of these and show people that if you are not sufficiently careful, someone will be more careful and make you look bad. It’s something I tell students all the time: you can be less careful and try to fudge things so they look good for you and get your paper published, but somebody’s going to really make you look bad a year or two later. You have to wait and wait and wait and hope that that never happens. One of the papers I talk about in this work was published in the same ICLR as the lottery ticket paper. Two or three years later, I wrote a paper that hopefully put that method to bed as something meaningful and useful. If you do a slightly shoddy job, you will have to live in fear for years that someone will finally call you out on it. It’s good to have papers like this every so often. Or I suppose sooner rather than later.

items.question: How do you think academic researchers should respond to the field’s shift toward large foundation models?
items.object: The shift toward large foundation models and its implications for academic research
items.answer: I mean, the field has changed. We’re focused on big foundation models these days as a field, in the same way that in 2017 or 2018 the field kind of narrowed to focus on deep learning and not all of machine learning. Now we’re focused on a small subset of deep learning. That’s totally okay. I just think we need to accept that. I think a lot of academia is in denial, or is in the bargaining stage right now, and we need to just kind of make our peace: this is where we are now, and adapt our questions accordingly. If you’re not working on these larger models and you’re not working on questions related to this right now, you’re not working on anything that’s going to be interesting or useful. I don’t know. You can accept that, or you’re still working on lottery tickets or adversarial examples for CIFAR-10 in 2023, in which case you need to ask yourself some fundamental questions about what you’re doing, quite frankly.

A lot of folks are pretty uncritical about what we’re working on and what the field is working on. If a lot of other people are working on it or someone important is working on it, then it must be an important topic.

items.question: How do you judge the research interest generated by Jeff Hinton’s lecture on the forward-forward algorithm?
items.object: Jeff Hinton’s forward-forward algorithm and scientific standards
items.answer: Jeff Hinton gives a lecture on this forward-forward algorithm, and then you see a bunch of papers on it even though he didn’t even present enough evidence in that talk to make it remotely compelling as a subject of study. We shouldn’t just take Jeff at his word; we should hold Jeff to the same standards as everybody else as a scientist. I think that’s a bad way to do things.

items.question: How do you decide which machine learning research questions are worth pursuing?
items.object: Choosing research topics: lottery tickets, data, and LLM evaluation
items.answer: The right way is to be self-critical and ask yourself whether you’re working on useful things or why you’re working on certain things. I’d like to hope that I’m very self-critical in that respect, personally. Why am I working on lottery tickets? I’m not anymore, and I tell my students not to work on lottery tickets because I don’t think it’s that useful. Why am I working on data these days? Because I think data is an important question as we get into these big networks. Why am I working on evaluation of LLMs these days? Because until we know how to evaluate what success looks like, we literally can’t answer any other question. I don’t know. Those are the questions that are calling to me right now, personally.

items.question: How did you decide what research idea Mosaic should be built around?
items.object: Mosaic’s research foundation
items.answer: I think it started when our now co-founders reached out to me and said, “Nice lottery ticket paper. Want to do a startup based on that?” You can imagine what I said, which was no, that’s not a good idea. But then eventually we talked about it and went, “Lottery ticket, maybe not.” From there, we talked about efficiency in general and whether there was room to still improve the algorithms and improve the way we train neural networks to reduce cost. The answer was yeah, there’s a lot of room for that, and then that’s where Mosaic started. It’s still the same empirical approach that we had in the lottery ticket paper.

items.question: What do you see as the core challenge in Mosaic’s business of helping people train large-scale models?
items.object: Mosaic’s business of making large-scale model training repeatable
items.answer: It sounds really boring. It is so hard to repeatedly, consistently train a great 30-billion-parameter model or 100-billion-parameter model or what have you, and we’ve built the tools to do that over and over again for diffusion models, for language models, and for a bunch of other stuff too. People come, they train, and they go. Sometimes they come back; oftentimes they come back and want to train something bigger. That’s really our business at the end of the day. We have to know how to train these big models, first of all, but second of all we have to build the tools in the product to make it repeatable. The one other thing I’ll throw in there is that involves reducing cost.

items.question: Why do you think people need to train custom models when publicly available models such as Llama 2 exist?
items.object: Custom models and the limits of publicly available models such as Llama 2
items.answer: I think a lot of folks need custom models at the end of the day. A lot of folks need, for various reasons, they’re working on a domain for which there doesn’t exist a model, or they just need something better than what exists publicly. Llama 2 is a perfectly good model, but people need more sometimes. People need something better or something very specialized for custom data, and in those cases you just got to train your own model. In some sense, my job is to make sure that’s possible. We certainly see this a lot.

items.question: How do you think about the time it takes for AI policy to develop?
items.object: The pace of AI policymaking
items.answer: I’ll say that policy takes time. It is not a fast process; it’s not designed to be a fast process, and you have to sometimes wait for the world to change as well. As an example, our work on police use of facial recognition came a half decade before a wave of amazing technical work on the part of other folks, plus society getting into the right place for this to happen and this technology to legitimately get banned in a lot of jurisdictions. That took time. Policy does take time. The interest in AI is happening years after we and other folks first rang the bell that there might be concerns here. Again, that takes time, and that’s okay. In fact, that’s kind of by design to some extent.

items.question: What do you think needs to come before making policies and laws about AI’s role in society?
items.object: Policy, law, and AI’s role in society
items.answer: I think we have a lot of tricky questions to answer right now about what role we want AI to play in society. Before we worry about policy and laws and anything else, we need to ask ourselves fundamental questions about what we want. To me, policy is the art of asking what we want as a society; law is the art of actually putting it into practice. I like to be at the table and try to help people get technical information.

items.question: How do you see your role as a technologist in discussions about AI policy?
items.object: Technologists’ role in AI policy discussions
items.answer: We as technologists are not the center of this conversation. We have knowledge to contribute, but there are skilled people who are used to weighing these different interests in society and helping to chart a direction. We are here to help them; we are not here to run the process or tell people what to do, even though we as technologists tend to have a lot of hubris.

items.question: What do you think matters most in the debate over AI regulation?
items.object: The debate over AI regulation
items.answer: I care more about the outcomes, to be honest. Discourse is always messy; that’s just kind of how it goes in this field. The much more important question is: where do we end up? How do we regulate these models? What are the outcomes? Is our open-source model something we’re still allowed to do? Is it something we should do? I don’t know anymore. I kind of wonder. I think these are the important questions, not the nature of the discourse and who’s coming to which White House photo op and what Sam Altman is saying in front of Congress. Those are attempts to influence the process, but the much more important part starts with: what do we even want?
